text.p: New technology is changing the face of market research, with the Internet, interactive television and telephones with video screens replacing paper questionnaires and phone surveys, experts said on Thursday.

Market research ranging from traditional newspaper readership polls to global surveys testing demand for new electronic products is being conducted via a variety of new media, according to speakers at a business conference.

The marketing use of new electronic technologies remains in its infancy, but experts at the Market Research Society's annual conference said they expected new-styled surveys to become as common as phone surveys.
"The paper and pencil interview is definitely on its way out," Chris Blamires, a partner of the Decision Modelling Consultancy, told delegates in Birmingham.
Conducting surveys over the Internet and using electronic technology can sharply cut costs of hiring pollsters and result in higher response rates and quicker response times, researchers said.

Alan Higgs, director of NOP Consumer Market Research, said response rates to traditional surveys had also dropped dramatically and people were increasingly reluctant to agree to door-to-door interviews.

He said a new kind of "screen telephone" that combines a personal computer with an ordinary phone helped address that problem and represented another way in which market research was entering the digital age.
NOP Consumer Market Research, an affiliate of Britain's Express Newspapers, which is owned by United News & Media Plc , is testing the phones for consumer surveys.
The screen phones were developed by Dutch electronics maker Philips Electronics NV.

NOP approached Philips about using the screen phones in a pilot project ahead of Philips' plans to sell the new devices later this year. The phones are expected to retail for about 250 pounds ($400) each.

Higgs said the screen phones meant market researchers could survey consumers without spending a lot of money on interviewers and the new devices allowed participants to answer surveys at their leisure.
"It's really a personal computer disguised as a telephone," he told the conference.
The phone, designed primarily for home shopping and banking, and equipped with a small video screen and keyboard, has been installed in the homes of 80 Express newspaper readers.
NOP hopes to expand the pilot programme and conduct surveys for other clients using the screen phone.
Other companies are using the Internet to do global surveys on new products and other subjects.

A market research expert from Reuters Holdings Plc said the international news and information group had done some market surveys on the Internet and other surveys on the company's own intranet -- its internal computer network that uses Internet technology. Nicky Perrott, head of market research and analysis for Reuters in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, told the conference surveys on the Internet and corporate intranets could save a lot of time and money.
She said a recent survey of employees on Reuters intranet generated a response rate of 56 percent in half the time a similar paper-based survey took to generate a response rate of only 14 percent.
Perrott said a different Reuters survey conducted over the Internet to test the market for a new electronic newspaper was done at a fraction of the cost of a traditional survey.
This week's conference in Birmingham covered a market research industry that is growing fast.

Manufacturers, service-industry companies and the ad agencies they hire face growing competition in Western consumer markets and are turning increasingly to market research experts to find out what consumers want to buy. ($ = 0.624 British Pounds Sterling)
